slides.title: The Six Core Principles
slides.subtitle: Governance standards for OrchestrAI delivery models

analogy.title: Mandatory Operational Controls
analogy.text: Similar to regulatory compliance controls, these six principles are mandatory. Skipping a control invalidates the governance framework, leading to developmental drift and unversioned code.

slides.memory_hook: Six principles. Zero exceptions. Governed delivery.

list.name: AI as Primary Builder
list.desc: AI writes ALL the code — APIs, schemas, UI, tests. If the Lead is writing code, something has gone wrong. Full stop.

list.name: Human as Orchestrator
list.desc: You define direction, constraints, trade-offs, and approvals. You're the conductor from Module 1 — not the violinist.

list.name: Plain-English Driven
list.desc: Requirements enter as natural language. No UML diagrams, no 47-page spec docs. Precise — but in plain English.

list.name: Continuous Delivery
list.desc: No sprints. No sprint planning. No retros about retros. Work flows continuously through the intent-validate-evolve loop.

list.name: Instant Iteration
list.desc: Gap found during validation? Fixed same session. Not next sprint. Not next quarter. Right now.

list.name: Quality by Design
list.desc: Security, validation, error handling — specified as constraints in the intent. Generated with every artifact from day one.

slides.narration: The OrchestrAI governance framework is built on six core principles. First: AI as Primary Builder. The AI engine generates all code artifacts; manual intervention breaks version control. Second: Human as Orchestrator. The Lead defines parameters and controls quality. Third: Plain-English Driven. Requirements are structured in precise natural language. Fourth: Continuous Delivery. Delivery is continuous rather than boxed into sprints. Fifth: Instant Iteration. Code correction happens in real-time. And sixth: Quality by Design. Security and validation are defined in the intent statement.

slides.narration: To understand this operational model, we compare traditional roles with OrchestrAI. In traditional models, the Lead patches code when AI fails. In OrchestrAI, the Lead re-prompts, never touching code directly. Traditional requirements are documented in bulky BRDs, whereas OrchestrAI uses plain-English briefs. Planning poker is replaced by continuous hourly loops. Security is baked in from the start, and documentation is auto-generated with the code, ensuring auditability.

slides.subtitle: Identify which core principle is violated in each scenario

cards.label: The Lead fixes a CSS bug directly in VS Code
cards.reveal: Violation: AI as Primary Builder. Re-prompt with a targeted correction instead. The moment you touch code, you break the audit trail.

cards.label: Team decides to 'just do one sprint' for the complex module
cards.reveal: Violation: Continuous Delivery. Even complex features flow through the intent-validate-evolve loop. Sprints are the old world's crutch.

cards.label: AI generates code without any security constraints in the prompt
cards.reveal: Violation: Quality by Design. Security isn't added later — it's a Marker in every intent. This output ships insecure by default.

cards.label: The Lead writes a 30-page BRD before any generation
cards.reveal: Violation: Plain-English Driven. Requirements are structured briefs, not enterprise documents. Precision, yes. Bureaucracy, no.

slides.subtitle: Quantifying the impact of skipping controls

hero_stat.label: the rework cost when even ONE principle is skipped

bullets: Skip 'AI as Primary Builder'? Manual code breaks the audit trail. Nobody can trace what was generated vs patched.
Skip 'Plain-English Driven'? You re-introduce the 47-page BRD cycle. Congratulations, you just rebuilt waterfall.
Skip 'Continuous Delivery'? Sprint ceremonies return. Velocity debates return. Four-month timelines return.
Skip 'Quality by Design'? Security becomes a late-stage surprise. Hallucinations ship undetected.
slides.closing_thread: Six rules, all six, every time. Now let's look at the actual machine that runs inside them.

analogy.title: The Compliance Paradigm
analogy.text: In regulatory audits, a single failed control invalidates the entire compliance certificate. Similarly, breaking one OrchestrAI principle compromises delivery safety. We enforce controls not for convenience, but to maintain architectural integrity.

slides.memory_hook: Principle deviations compound rework costs and compromise delivery speed.
slides.narration: Operational data shows that rework costs increase three-fold when even a single principle is bypassed. If you bypass AI as Primary Builder, you lose code auditability. Bypassing Plain-English Driven re-introduces document-heavy waterfall processes. Bypassing Continuous Delivery forces teams back into artificial sprint boxes. And bypassing Quality by Design creates late-stage security risks. Governance is essential to maintain delivery velocity.

analogy.title: Dynamic Process Models
analogy.text: A static delivery model follows a rigid sequence regardless of outcomes. A dynamic model, like a modern workflow router, shifts execution based on real-time feedback. The OrchestrAI lifecycle loops constantly to integrate feedback immediately.

slides.memory_hook: I-O-G-V-E-D: Intent, Orchestrate, Generate, Validate, Evolve, Deploy. The engine of delivery.

list.name: INTENT
list.desc: Define what you're building with surgical precision. This is where P.R.O.M.P.T. from Module 1 meets enterprise requirements.

list.name: ORCHESTRATE
list.desc: Map the dependency graph. What needs to exist first? Which components, in what order, with what API contracts?

list.name: GENERATE
list.desc: AI builds. You direct. One focused prompt per component — not one giant prompt for the whole system.

list.name: VALIDATE
list.desc: Systematic check against acceptance criteria. Not a vibe check — a checklist.

list.name: EVOLVE
list.desc: Stakeholder feedback → new intent → re-generate → re-validate. Same session, not next sprint.

list.name: DEPLOY
list.desc: Continuous, governed, documented, reversible. Not a 'project-end event' — a daily activity.

Stage five: Evolve. Feedback is rapidly integrated in the same session. Stage six: Deploy. Code is released continuously in a governed, auditable manner.

slides.title: Stage 1: INTENT — Architectural Foundations
slides.subtitle: Precision in requirements prevents drift in generated artifacts
bullets: Outcome: Specify the desired runtime behavior in a single sentence
Actor & Role: Enumerate access privileges and constraints
Validation Rules: Define explicit conditions for input correctness
Security Constraints: Establish client and server-side enforcement
Acceptance Signals: Define measurable criteria for success verification
Edge Cases: Map boundary conditions and error state expectations
Stack & Patterns: Provide structural technology constraints
slides.closing_thread: These components compose the structured intent framework, scaling Module 1's P.R.O.M.P.T. method.

analogy.title: Foundation Engineering
analogy.text: In civil engineering, minor alignment deviations at the foundation level compound into structural failures at higher stories. In AI delivery, an incomplete intent brief guarantees drift in the generated code.

slides.memory_hook: Precise intent structures guarantee predictable generated code. Define constraints upfront.
slides.narration: In Stage one: Intent, precision is paramount. A minor requirements omission compounds into severe code drift. slides.subtitle: Evaluating the outcomes of weak versus structured briefs
slides.memory_hook: Same P.R.O.M.P.T. idea from Module 1 — but enterprise-grade now. Eight components, not six.

before.label: Weak Intent
before.output: 'Build a timesheet entry screen where users can log hours against projects.' → AI assumes scope, skips validation rules, creates its own schema, doesn't enforce anything server-side. You spend 2 days fixing what should've taken 2 hours.

after.label: Strong Intent (8 Components)
after.output: 'Build a timesheet entry screen for Team Members (role: TEAM_MEMBER). 7-day grid, Mon-Sun, rows for project/task pairs. 10 validation rules: (1) at least one complete row, (2) project mandatory, (3) task mandatory, (4) no duplicate project+task, (5) daily hours 0-24, (6) task not expired, (7-8) no hours outside task date range, (9) daily total <=24h, (10) weekly total >=40h. Enforced client AND server-side. First failed rule shows persistent red banner. Submit disabled until clean save. Stack: React + TypeScript, NestJS, Prisma, PostgreSQL.' → Ships same day. Zero rework.

slides.title: Stage 2: ORCHESTRATE — Dependency Architecture
slides.subtitle: Structuring the compilation sequence

analogy.title: Critical Path Analysis
analogy.text: A project manager does not schedule UI design ahead of core systems architecture. We must identify the critical path. In OrchestrAI, this means establishing data schemas and API structures before generating consumer components.

slides.memory_hook: Dependency analysis precedes code generation. Plan the sequence.

list.name: Dependency Graph
list.desc: What must exist before this feature can be built? Auth before user profiles. Database before API. API before UI.

list.name: Reusable Components
list.desc: What already exists in the codebase? Don't regenerate what works — assemble from proven patterns.

list.name: API Contract
list.desc: What endpoints? What request/response shapes? What auth guards? Define before generation, not after.

list.name: Data Model
list.desc: New tables, columns, relationships, indices, constraints — all mapped before a single prompt fires.

list.name: Cross-Cutting Concerns
list.desc: Logging, error handling patterns, naming conventions. These apply everywhere — specify once, enforce always.

slides.narration: Stage two is Orchestrate. Before beginning generation, the Lead maps the dependency sequence. Database schemas must be generated first, followed by services, API endpoints, and finally, frontend components. We identify reusable logic in the codebase, document API contracts, design data schemas, and define cross-cutting concerns like security logging. This structure prevents refactoring loops.

slides.title: Stage 3: GENERATE — Supervising Code Construction
slides.subtitle: Maintaining control through granular prompting and real-time oversight
bullets: One focused prompt per component. NOT one mega-prompt for the entire system.
Always include context: existing code patterns, naming conventions, stack version.
Review output IMMEDIATELY — don't queue multiple generations before validating the first.
If AI deviates, correct with a targeted constraint prompt. Never accept and fix manually.
Never accept code you can't explain. If you can't explain it, you can't validate it.
slides.closing_thread: Generated? Great. Now comes the real job — validation.

analogy.title: Control Room Operations
analogy.text: A reactor supervisor does not step away while automated systems execute adjustments. They monitor indicators in real-time, intervening at the first variance. The Lead operates with identical oversight during AI code generation.

slides.memory_hook: Granular prompts. Real-time review. No batch generations.
slides.narration: Stage three is Generate. The Lead acts as an active supervisor rather than a passive observer. We review output immediately, and if the AI engine deviates, we apply targeted constraint corrections. Under no circumstances do we accept code we cannot fully explain.

slides.title: Validate, Evolve, and Deploy
slides.subtitle: Quality assurance, rapid iteration, and rollout governance

analogy.title: Quality Audit and Release Operations
analogy.text: Validate acts as the pre-delivery audit. Evolve represents final adjustments based on stakeholder reviews. Deploy operates as the controlled rollout. Each step must adhere to governance standards before code is certified for release.

slides.memory_hook: Validate systematically. Evolve in-session. Deploy continuously with rollbacks.

list.name: VALIDATE — The Checklist, Not the Vibe
list.desc: Check every acceptance criterion explicitly. Functional, security, data isolation, error handling, edge cases, documentation. If it's not on the checklist, it's not validated.

list.name: EVOLVE — Same-Session Enhancement
list.desc: Stakeholder sees it in the demo → gives feedback → you reshape intent → AI regenerates → you revalidate. Hours, not sprints.

list.name: DEPLOY — Continuous, Not Ceremonial
list.desc: Deploy to staging when validated. Deploy to production when quality threshold met. Every deployment documented, tested, reversible.

slides.narration: We now review the final stages of the lifecycle. Validation requires testing against a systematic checklist covering functionality, security, data isolation, and error states. slides.title: The 8-Component Intent Framework
slides.subtitle: The structured specification template for enterprise features

analogy.title: ISO Certification Controls
analogy.text: An ISO compliance audit requires documented proof for every control. Skipping a single item invalidates the certification. The 8-component intent framework operates with equivalent rigour — every component must be complete.

slides.memory_hook: Outcome, Actor, Validation, Security, Stack, Acceptance, Edge, Data. Ensure all 8 are defined.

list.name: Outcome
list.desc: One sentence: what working behaviour should exist? This is Purpose from P.R.O.M.P.T., levelled up.

list.name: Actor & Role
list.desc: Exact user role, their permissions, and what they CANNOT do.

list.name: Validation Rules
list.desc: Every rule that determines valid vs invalid input, numbered.

list.name: Security Constraints
list.desc: Auth, authorization, enforcement layer — always both client AND server-side.

list.name: Stack & Patterns
list.desc: Technology, version, naming conventions, existing patterns to follow.

list.name: Acceptance Signals
list.desc: Explicit list of what success looks like. If you can't test it, it's not an acceptance signal.

list.name: Edge Cases
list.desc: Boundary conditions, error states, empty states, concurrent requests.

list.name: Data Model
list.desc: Tables, columns, relationships, constraints involved.

slides.narration: The structured intent framework consists of eight mandatory components. We specify the core Outcome in a single sentence, define the Actor roles and access rights, detail numbered Validation Rules, and set Security Constraints. We define the Stack and Patterns, establish testable Acceptance Signals, map out Edge Cases, and declare the Data Model. Omitting any component introduces delivery risks.

slides.title: Architectural Defect Analysis
slides.subtitle: Identify missing governance constraints in this requirements brief

flaws.explanation: No Validation Rules. What makes an expense valid? Required fields? Amount limits? Duplicate detection? Without numbered rules, AI will guess — and guess wrong.
No Security Constraints. Who enforces that a Manager can only see their team's expenses? Client-side only? Server-side? Both? Without this, data leaks.
No Edge Cases. What if a Manager IS the submitter? What about expenses submitted after the period closes? What if the VP is on leave? These become production bugs.

slides.text: Build an expense approval workflow. Managers approve expenses submitted by their team. Expenses over ₹50,000 require VP approval. Use React + NestJS + PostgreSQL. The workflow should send email notifications on approval or rejection.

slides.title: Common Intent Anti-Patterns
slides.subtitle: Recognizing and mitigating common prompting errors

analogy.title: Vague Service Requests
analogy.text: Submitting an ambiguous work order to a contractor leads to cost overruns and incorrect materials. Software intent behaves identically. Vague specifications lead directly to structural drift and rework.

slides.memory_hook: Identify anti-patterns: Vague Outcomes, Mega-Prompts, Assumptions, Skip Testing, and Manual Patches.

list.name: The Vague Outcome
list.desc: 'Build a dashboard for managers.' No scope, no role def, no data spec. Fix: specify exact role, exact metrics, exact data sources, exact acceptance criteria.

list.name: The Mega-Prompt
list.desc: One prompt for the entire app. Quality degrades with scope. Fix: one focused prompt per component, validate each before next.

list.name: The Assumption Prompt
list.desc: 'Add authentication.' No stack, no existing patterns, no token strategy. Fix: specify exact mechanism, reference existing code.

list.name: The Trust-and-Skip
list.desc: Accepting output without checking. AI is statistically good but not always correct. Fix: validate every output. No exceptions.

list.name: The Manual Patch
list.desc: Fixing code by hand instead of re-prompting. Creates drift between intent and implementation. Fix: always correct through prompting.

slides.narration: We must avoid five common intent anti-patterns. First: the Vague Outcome, which lacks scope and specifications. Second: the Mega-Prompt, which attempts to generate large systems in a single pass, degrading output quality. Third: the Assumption Prompt, which fails to specify dependencies. Fourth: the Trust-and-Skip, which accepts code without verification. Fifth: the Manual Patch, which updates code directly, creating code drift.

slides.title: The Validation Checklist
slides.subtitle: A systematic quality gate for generated components

analogy.title: ISO Quality Audit Checklist
analogy.text: A certified quality auditor does not rely on subjective evaluations. They check and document compliance against defined criteria. Validation requires an identical approach — structured, systematic, and documented.

slides.memory_hook: Seven mandatory checks verify component security, logic, isolation, and integration.

list.name: Functional Correctness
list.desc: Does every acceptance criterion produce the correct behaviour? Test each one explicitly.

list.name: Business Rule Enforcement
list.desc: Is every validation rule enforced server-side, not only in the UI? Can it be bypassed via API?

list.name: Data Isolation
list.desc: Can User A see User B's data in any code path? Test cross-tenant access explicitly.

list.name: Error Handling
list.desc: Does every error return a clear, user-appropriate message? No stack traces, no internal paths.

list.name: Security
list.desc: Auth guards on every endpoint. Authorization at service layer. Parameterized queries. No PII in responses.

list.name: Edge Cases
list.desc: Empty inputs, boundary values, concurrent requests — all the edge cases from the intent.

list.name: Documentation
list.desc: Has auto-generated documentation accurately captured what was built, including decisions?

slides.narration: Validation must be systematic. The Lead executes a checklist of seven points before accepting code. Functional correctness verifies acceptance criteria. Business rule enforcement checks server-side constraints. Data isolation ensures users cannot access other tenants' records. We also test error handling, security configurations, edge cases, and ensure auto-generated documentation remains current.

slides.subtitle: Managing persistent code deviations and edge failures

analogy.title: Operational Triage Models

Technological limits are escalated to the Solution Architect, and unexplained code is rejected until clarified.

slides.title: Enterprise Delivery Workflow: Case Study
slides.subtitle: A step-by-step review of the six-stage loop

analogy.title: Structured Execution Review
analogy.text: A post-incident review walks through the chronological log to identify system behavior. We will review a standard feature rollout chronology, analyzing the operational progression across a single working shift.

slides.memory_hook: Chronological progression of a feature release across all six lifecycle stages.

timeline.desc: Stakeholder says: 'We need employees to submit expenses.' You turn that into a full 8-component intent with 6 validation rules, 3 roles, and server-side enforcement.
Expense table needs Employee table (exists). Approval workflow needs Manager role mapping (exists). Email service needs notification template (new).
Prompt 1: database migration. Prompt 2: service layer with business rules. Prompt 3: API endpoints with guards. Prompt 4: React form with validation. Each validated before next.
All 6 validation rules tested. Server-side enforcement confirmed. Manager can't see other teams' expenses. Error messages are clean. Edge cases covered.
Demo at 11:30. Stakeholder: 'Can we add receipt photo upload?' → New intent item → generate → validate → done by 2 PM.
Code committed with structured message. Docs auto-updated. Feature in client's QA by 4:30. Rollback plan documented.

slides.title: Living Documentation Standards
slides.subtitle: Integrating documentation into the automated generation pipeline
bullets: Documentation is generated ALONGSIDE the code, not after
It includes: what was built, what decisions were made, what constraints applied
Every commit message follows: [FEATURE] [Component] — AI-generated, validated by [Lead]
The Lead reviews auto-generated docs DAILY and flags inaccuracies
Documentation that falls behind the code = ungoverned code
slides.closing_thread: Every principle, every stage, every artifact — documented as it happens. Not after.

analogy.title: Audit Ledger vs. Manual Log
analogy.text: A database transaction log is written automatically at execution. A manual audit sheet requires operators to record events after the fact, introducing error risks. OrchestrAI documentation acts as a transaction log.

slides.memory_hook: Documentation is generated programmatically alongside code. Out-of-date docs equal untrusted code.
slides.narration: In OrchestrAI, documentation is generated alongside code, not after. It logs what was built, structural decisions, and API constraints. Commit messages use standard naming formats, and the Lead reviews auto-generated docs daily for accuracy. Out-of-date documentation is classified as ungoverned code, which violates release protocols.

slides.title: Module 2 Executive Summary
slides.subtitle: Key takeaways for framework architecture
bullets: Six principles govern every engagement. Break one, it's not OrchestrAI.
The lifecycle is a loop, not a line: Intent → Orchestrate → Generate → Validate → Evolve → Deploy.
Intent is the foundation — eight components, all eight, every time.
Validation is a systematic checklist, not a vibe check.
Documentation lives alongside the code — generated, not written after.
slides.closing_thread: Knowledge assessment follows. 80% passing grade required.

slides.title: Module 2 Knowledge Assessment
slides.subtitle: Verify governance and architectural understanding

questions.question: Which principle is violated when a Lead manually fixes a bug in AI-generated code instead of re-prompting?
questions.explanation: Manual code fixes break the audit trail and create drift between intent and implementation. Always correct through re-prompting.

questions.question: 'No sprints, no sprint planning, no retros' — which principle?
questions.explanation: Continuous Delivery means work flows through the intent-validate-evolve loop in hours, replacing fixed-time sprint boxes.

questions.question: Quality by Design means security and validation are specified WHERE?
choices: In the intent statement, as constraints before generation
During the validate stage after generation
By a QA engineer in staging
questions.correct_answer: In the intent statement, as constraints before generation
questions.explanation: Quality by Design requires security and validation rules to be specified upfront as constraints in the intent, so they are built in from day one.

questions.question: What is the correct order of the six lifecycle stages?
choices: Intent -> Orchestrate -> Generate -> Validate -> Evolve -> Deploy
Orchestrate -> Intent -> Generate -> Validate -> Evolve -> Deploy
Intent -> Generate -> Orchestrate -> Validate -> Evolve -> Deploy
Intent -> Orchestrate -> Generate -> Evolve -> Validate -> Deploy
questions.correct_answer: Intent -> Orchestrate -> Generate -> Validate -> Evolve -> Deploy
questions.explanation: The lifecycle always starts with Intent, maps dependencies in Orchestrate, generates with AI, validates against checklist, evolves from feedback, and deploys daily.

questions.question: During the ORCHESTRATE stage, the Lead's primary job is to:
choices: Map the dependency graph and define the component build order
Test the UI for CSS bugs
questions.correct_answer: Map the dependency graph and define the component build order
questions.explanation: Orchestration is about laying out the dependency analysis and assembly sequence (database before service before API before UI).

questions.question: What should a Lead do if AI output still deviates after 3 targeted re-prompts?
choices: Pause generation and engage the SME/architect for review
Fix the code manually in VS Code
Skip this feature and build something else
questions.correct_answer: Pause generation and engage the SME/architect for review
questions.explanation: If generation fails three times, pause. Escalation is professional judgment. Get an SME or architect to review the intent structure.

questions.question: How many components does a perfect intent statement have?
questions.explanation: The 8-component framework consists of: Outcome, Actor & Role, Validation Rules, Security Constraints, Stack & Patterns, Acceptance Signals, Edge Cases, and Data Model.

questions.question: Which anti-pattern involves issuing one massive prompt for an entire application?
questions.explanation: The Mega-Prompt degrades quality with scope. The rule is: one focused prompt per component, validating each before moving on.

questions.question: Which validation category checks whether User A can see User B's data?
questions.explanation: Data Isolation validation explicitly tests database querying and controller scope to ensure cross-tenant data leaks cannot occur.

questions.question: What MUST be true before any AI-generated code reaches production?
choices: Lead validation sign-off, security checklist pass, test pass, docs current, rollback plan
The code compiles and seems to work in the UI
The AI says the code is complete and secure
The project manager approves the design layout
questions.correct_answer: Lead validation sign-off, security checklist pass, test pass, docs current, rollback plan
questions.explanation: Deployments in OrchestrAI must be governed, documented, tested, and reversible, with current living documentation.

slides.title: Case Study 1: Lifecycle Mapping
slides.subtitle: Deconstruct business requirements into structured specifications

scenario.label: The Scenario
scenario.text: A client says: 'We need a leave request system. Employees request leave, managers approve or reject, and HR can see all requests.' That's the entire brief. Your job: write the INTENT (8 components) and the ORCHESTRATION plan (dependency order + API contracts) before a single prompt fires.

slides.task_prompt: Construct the 8-component intent brief and sequence the development order for the leave request system.

input_fields.label: Outcome
input_fields.placeholder: One sentence: what working behaviour should exist?

input_fields.label: Actor & Role
input_fields.placeholder: List all user roles and their permissions

input_fields.label: Validation Rules (numbered)
input_fields.placeholder: What makes input valid or invalid?

input_fields.label: Build Order (numbered)
input_fields.placeholder: What gets generated first, second, third...?

input_fields.label: Key API Endpoints
input_fields.placeholder: List the main endpoints with HTTP verbs and guards

model_answer.outcome: Build a leave request system where Employees submit requests, Managers approve/reject team requests, and HR views all requests.
model_answer.actor_role: EMPLOYEE (request leave, view own history), MANAGER (view/approve/reject team leave), HR (view all leave requests, no edit).
model_answer.validation_rules: (1) leave dates must be in future, (2) start date <= end date, (3) description mandatory, (4) leave duration cannot exceed remaining balance.
model_answer.security: JWT auth. Managers can only access requests where submitter's managerId matches Manager's ID. HR role required for global read endpoint.
model_answer.build_order: (1) Prisma schema with LeaveRequest model and migrations, (2) NestJS Service layer with validation rules, (3) Controller endpoints with Guards, (4) React forms and tables.
model_answer.api_contracts: POST /leave (Employee, submit), GET /leave/team (Manager, view team), PATCH /leave/:id/approve (Manager, action), GET /leave/all (HR, view all).

comparison_report.title: How did your plan stack up?
comparison_report.intro: This lab tests your ability to structure intent and define a clean build sequence before prompting. Let's compare your plan to the model answer.

common_gaps.insight: Did you catch that Managers must be restricted to their own team? Client-side hidden lists aren't enough — it must be enforced server-side via SQL/ORM conditions.
Database migrations must come first. Generating controllers before the schema results in import errors and compiler noise.

comparison_report.closing_line: Review the differences and proceed to Lab 2 when you're ready.

slides.title: Case Study 2: Validation Engineering
slides.subtitle: Establish systematic testing criteria for generated components

scenario.label: The Scenario
scenario.text: Using the leave request feature from Lab 1, your AI just generated the service layer and API endpoints. Before you accept this code, you need a validation checklist. For each acceptance criterion below, write the specific test action you'd perform.

slides.task_prompt: Declare specific, executable validation checks for each criterion listed.

input_fields.label: Functional Test
input_fields.placeholder: How do you verify an employee can submit a leave request?

input_fields.label: Business Rule Test
input_fields.placeholder: How do you verify overlapping leave dates are rejected?

input_fields.label: Data Isolation Test
input_fields.placeholder: How do you verify Employee A can't see Employee B's requests?

input_fields.label: Security Test
input_fields.placeholder: How do you verify the API rejects unauthenticated requests?

input_fields.label: Edge Case Test
input_fields.placeholder: What happens when an employee requests leave for a past date?

input_fields.label: Error Handling Test
input_fields.placeholder: What does the user see when submitting an invalid request?

model_answer.functional: Use Swagger/Postman to POST a valid leave request payload as Employee A. Verify 201 Created response and DB record existence.
model_answer.business_rule: Submit a leave request for July 1-5, then submit another for July 3-7 for same Employee. Verify 400 Bad Request on second.
model_answer.data_isolation: Log in as Manager A. Attempt GET /leave/team. Verify only requests from Employee A (team member) are returned, no Employee B (Manager B's team) requests.
model_answer.security: Make GET /leave/all request without Authorization header. Verify 401 Unauthorized response is returned.
model_answer.edge_case: Submit leave request with startDate in past (e.g. yesterday). Verify API validation rejects it with clear validation error.
model_answer.error_handling: Submit a request missing dates. Verify response contains detailed JSON error list showing validation errors, not a 500 error.

comparison_report.title: Checklist Validation
comparison_report.intro: A true OrchestrAI Lead tests systematically. Let's compare your validation test actions with the model answers.

common_gaps.insight: Always test with cross-tenant context. Trying to fetch data using another user's ID is the absolute best way to check if your server-side checks actually hold up.
Ensure bad payloads return 400 with messages. If you get a 500 response, that's a validation leak — the database crashed instead of the API catching it.

comparison_report.closing_line: Compare your checks, confirm you understand, and let's unlock that final certificate slide!
